newsitem.title: USA: IMF may stop short of explicitly backing gold sale.
newsitem.headline: IMF may stop short of explicitly backing gold sale.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund Wednesday looked set to endorse stepped-up aid to the world's poorest countries without explicitly spelling out how to finance it, international monetary sources said.

That would effectively leave open the question of whether the IMF would sell five million ounces of gold as part of program to beef up its Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility and provide debt relief to poor countries.
The sources stressed that the IMF board was still meeting and that the final outcome was still not totally certain.

IMF management, backed by the United States, Britain and most other member nations, has proposed selling five million of the fund's 104 million ounces of gold if needed to help finance stepped-up assistance to poor countries.
But a few nations -- Germany, Italy and Switzerland -- have opposed the proposal, arguing in part that the IMF should not sell gold except in cases of extreme financial emergency.

The monetary sources, who declined to be named, said they expect the IMF board to pledge to come up with the necessary financing for the continuation of the ESAF lending facility and the debt relief initiative for the world's poor.
But the sources said the board looks unlikely to specifically endorse the sale of IMF gold if needed to fill the financing gap, which is estimated at some $3.5 billion from the year 2000 to 2004.
The IMF could shift some money from its ESAF reserves -- perhaps something on the order of $700 million -- to meet part of the financing commitment.
Bilateral contributions from major nations would also be available, but proponents of gold sales argue that will not be enough to provide all the money that is needed.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told reporters earlier today that gold sales would be needed to finance the stepped-up IMF aid that is planned for world's poor.
"When you get finished with all the modalities, it's the only way to do this," he said.
"We will continue to work toward an agreement to sell gold if that in fact is the only way we can help poor governments," he added.
